1100.title: The eight, in depth
1100.hook: the poor, the needy, collectors, hearts to be reconciled, freeing captives, debtors, Allah's cause, travelers (9:60)
1100.howItsDone: Muslims give zakat only to the eight kinds of recipients named in Qur'an 9:60, directly or through mosques and zakat organizations that distribute it among them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harvest's tenth: rain's share. A week about what's given; today, who it goes to.

A single verse, surah nine, verse sixty, and it reads like a guest list. Not a vague one. Not give to good causes. It names who, one after another, and then it stops. Some of the names are obvious. Some are surprising. One is a person who's simply far from home. You met this list on day one fifty-two, in one breath. Today, read slowly, two by two: the eight.
screen: `ONE VERSE, LIKE A GUEST LIST.` → `IT NAMES WHO, THEN STOPS.` → `READ SLOWLY, TWO BY TWO.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse in Pickthall's words: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy, and those who collect them, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and to free the captives and the debtors, and for the cause of Allah, and (for) the wayfarer; a duty imposed by Allah." First pair: the poor and the needy, al-fuqara' and al-masakin. Both lack enough, and scholars discuss which of the two is worse off, without one settled answer. Either way, they come first in the verse. Second pair: those who collect it, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled. The collectors are paid from zakat for their work, so the system can run. The hearts to be reconciled are people whose goodwill toward the community was being won, and scholars differ on how this door applies today. Third pair: freeing captives, and debtors. Money that buys someone's freedom, and money that lifts a crushing debt off someone's back. Both get a person out from under something. Fourth pair: the cause of Allah, and the wayfarer. Some scholars read the cause of Allah narrowly, others more broadly, and that difference matters for where zakat goes. The wayfarer, ibn as-sabil, literally son of the road, is a traveler cut off from their money, even someone wealthy at home. So zakat isn't only for people who are always poor. It's for anyone stranded. And notice the word only at the start. The list is a boundary: these eight, and not just any good cause.

The eight. The people zakat is for, named in surah nine, verse sixty, from the poor to the wayfarer. Today's word.
Your line: eight doors. A person can walk through any one of them. Tomorrow: the fifth, a share some Muslims give alongside zakat.

1101.title: The fifth
1101.hook: in Shia law, a fifth of yearly surplus is also due, half for the Imam's share through scholars, half for needy descendants of the Prophet ﷺ
1101.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims set a yearly khums date, calculate a fifth of the surplus left after the year's expenses, and pay it through the office of the marja' they follow; Sunni Muslims apply a fifth to found treasure and pay zakat on their savings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eight doors zakat goes through. Today, a second share that Twelver Shia Muslims keep alongside it.

A family in a Shia home sits down on a set day of the year with a notebook. Not their zakat day; another one. They add up what came in over the year and subtract what the year cost: rent, food, school, the car repair, the gifts for Eid. Whatever is left, the surplus the year didn't need, they divide by five. One part of five is not theirs to keep. Some goes, through the office of a senior scholar they follow, to the work of religion. Some goes to needy families descended from the Prophet ﷺ. Today, the fifth: khums.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK, ONCE A YEAR.` → `WHAT CAME IN, MINUS WHAT IT COST.` → `ONE PART OF FIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. Surah eight, verse forty-one, speaks of whatever you take as gains, and says a fifth of it belongs to Allah and the messenger, to the near kin, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. Both communities read the same verse, but read one of its words differently. Second, the Sunni reading. Sunni scholars read the verse about the spoils taken in war, a fifth of which was set aside for these purposes. They also apply it to buried treasure someone finds: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives found treasure a fifth. Beyond those, Sunni law asks zakat, not khums, of ordinary savings. Third, the Shia reading. Twelver Shia scholars read the verse's word for gains broadly, as any gain, relying on reports from the Imams of the Prophet's family that apply it to a person's yearly profit. So in Twelver Shia law, a fifth of the year's surplus is due, after the year's real expenses, alongside zakat. Their jurists divide it in two. Half is the share of the Imam, given today through a senior scholar, a marja', to support religious learning and the community. Half is for needy descendants of the Prophet ﷺ, who in this teaching may not receive zakat from those outside the family. Fourth: both readings start from the same verse, and both send the share to the near kin, the orphan, the needy and the traveler. The difference is in a word and in the scholars each community follows, and each gives its reasons. A friend who pays khums is following their law, as a friend who doesn't is following theirs.

1102.title: With dignity
1102.hook: zakat is the right of the poor, not a favor, and given with respect
1102.howItsDone: Muslim teachers describe zakat as the poor's due rather than a favor, and stress giving it without reminders, public display or wounding words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, khums, a fifth of the surplus: in Twelver Shia law, a fifth of what the year didn't need is set aside.

A woman stands at the counter of a food pantry. The volunteer is kind, but there's a clipboard, a line of people behind her, and a question asked loud enough for the line to hear. She gets the bag. She also gets the feeling of having been looked at. Nobody did anything wrong, exactly. And yet she walks out smaller than she walked in. The Qur'an has a word about this moment, and it isn't about the food. It's about who the food belonged to before it changed hands.
screen: `A COUNTER, A CLIPBOARD, A LINE.` → `SHE GETS THE BAG.` → `WHOSE FOOD WAS IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the word the Qur'an uses. In surah fifty-one, describing people of faith, Pickthall's translation says: "And in their wealth the beggar and the outcast had due share." The Arabic word is haqq: a right, something owed. Surah seventy says it again: the wealth of the faithful holds "a right acknowledged" for the one who asks and the one who goes without. So in this way of seeing it, the giver isn't doing the poor a favor. Their share was already inside the giver's money. Zakat hands it over. Second, if it's their right, how it's given matters. Surah two is direct: "A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury." The next verse warns believers not to make their almsgiving worthless by reminding people of it, or by hurting them. Giving and then lording it over someone empties the gift. Third, the text praises giving that stays hidden. Surah two says giving openly is good, but giving in secret to the poor is better for you. Some teachers connect this to the person receiving: when nobody watches, nobody is shamed. Fourth, the counter itself. Life can put anyone on either side of it. The one holding the bag of groceries is asked to remember they're returning something, not bestowing it. That changes the voice you use, where you stand, whether you make someone wait in front of a crowd. So the woman at the pantry, in this reading, is not a charity case. She's collecting what was hers.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last time you gave something to someone who needed it, money, food, a ride, your time, and replay it slowly: where you stood, whether you looked them in the eye, whether you mentioned it afterward. 1103.title: Zakat and sadaqah
1103.hook: zakat is required and measured; sadaqah is any gift, any time
1103.howItsDone: Muslims pay zakat once a year on qualifying wealth, and give sadaqah whenever they choose, in money, food, help or kind words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving with dignity: their right. The poor's share already sits inside the giver's wealth, and it's handed over without reminders.

A smile at the bus stop. A rock kicked off the sidewalk so nobody trips. A bill that comes due once a year, worked out to the decimal. Which of these is charity? According to sayings of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, all of them can be. But only one is zakat. Two of Islam's words for giving sit side by side like two hands. One is measured, owed and dated. The other has no amount, no season and no minimum.
screen: `A SMILE. A ROCK. A YEARLY BILL.` → `ALL CHARITY?` → `TWO WORDS FOR GIVING.`

segments.voice: First, zakat, as these past days have walked through it: a pillar, owed once wealth passes the threshold, measured by a rate, due on a yearly date, sent to the eight groups the Qur'an names. Second, sadaqah, with no fixed amount and no fixed day. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet ﷺ says every good deed is sadaqah. Other reports fill in the list: removing something harmful from the road, a good word, and, in a report in at-Tirmidhi, smiling in your brother's face. Third, the two overlap, and the language shows it. The verse naming the eight groups who receive zakat, surah nine, verse sixty, actually uses sadaqat, the plural of sadaqah. Pickthall translates it simply: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy." That verse is read as the list for zakat. So the line between the words isn't a wall: zakat is a sadaqah made obligatory and given a measure. Fourth, what if someone has nothing to give? Another report in Bukhari takes that head on. Every Muslim owes sadaqah, the Prophet ﷺ says. The companions ask: and if a person has nothing? Then work with your hands, benefit yourself, and give. And if they can't? Help someone in need. And if not that? Do good and hold back from harm; that counts as sadaqah too. So a single day can hold two kinds of giving: a duty with a calculator, and one open all day that costs as little as a kind face.

1104.title: Zakat institutions
1104.hook: mosques and charities collect and distribute zakat today
1104.howItsDone: Muslims pay zakat directly to people in need or through mosques, community funds, charities and, in some countries, government zakat agencies, which collect it and distribute it to the eight groups named in the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday, zakat and sadaqah: required and freely. One gift is measured and owed; the other is open all day.

In the last days of Ramadan, a table goes up near a mosque door: a box, a card reader, a QR code on the wall, a volunteer with a sheet of numbers. Elsewhere, a charity's website has a zakat calculator and a page saying where last year's money went. The person paying and the family receiving never meet. So who carries the gift across? The Qur'an's own list of who receives zakat has an answer: the people who collect it.
screen: `A TABLE BY THE MOSQUE DOOR.` → `A CALCULATOR ON A WEBSITE.` → `WHO CARRIES THE GIFT ACROSS?`

segments.voice: First, the collectors are in the text. Surah nine, verse sixty, lists the eight groups zakat may go to, and among them, in Pickthall's words, "those who collect them." Collecting and handing out zakat is work, and the Qur'an makes room to pay those who do it from zakat itself. Second, it was a task given to the Prophet himself. In surah nine, verse one hundred three, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." When he sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal to Yemen, the report in Sahih al-Bukhari says he told him to teach that zakat is taken from their rich and given back to their poor. Their rich, their poor: some scholars read that as keeping zakat close to where it was collected. Third, today the hands differ from country to country: a government agency, a local mosque, a community fund, a charity working across borders. Scholars discuss the questions these bodies face: whether zakat can go to a poor family far away when there's need nearby, and how much can pay running costs. Schools and scholars answer differently, and a good zakat charity will tell you which scholars it follows. Fourth, the giver's part. Giving through an institution isn't less personal; it can reach someone you'd never find alone. But the giver still asks where it goes, and trusts the hands it passes through. That closes these days on zakat: a chain of people carrying a right to the one it belongs to.

1105.title: The intention to fast
1105.hook: the intention for Ramadan, made each night or once for the month, by school
1105.howItsDone: Muslims make the intention to fast in the heart before dawn; Shafi'i and Hanbali Muslims renew it each night of Ramadan, Malikis may make one intention for the month, and Hanafis may make it until around midday for a Ramadan fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the days on zakat: given through many hands, from the collectors named in surah nine to the charities of today.

Skip breakfast and lunch, and by afternoon the body can't tell why. Too busy to eat? Or fasting? Same empty stomach, same slump, same glance at the clock. The difference is invisible, and it happened before the day began: someone decided. The Islamic fast begins not at dawn with the first hunger but earlier, in the mind, with a word the legal books set at the start of acts of worship. Today, the intention to fast.
screen: `AN EMPTY STOMACH BY AFTERNOON.` → `FORGOT, OR FASTED?` → `THE DIFFERENCE CAME FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the command. Surah two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." The fast has a purpose, and a purpose needs someone who means it. Second, the word is niyyah, intention. The collection of Imam al-Bukhari opens with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. That's why a forgotten lunch and a fast aren't the same. A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others ties this to fasting: whoever doesn't resolve to fast before dawn has no fast. Third, how often? Here the schools differ. Some, such as the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, teach that the intention for each obligatory day of Ramadan is made each night, before dawn. The Maliki school holds that one intention at the start of the month can cover it all, as long as the fast isn't broken off. The Hanafi school allows a Ramadan day's intention later, before about the middle of the day, if nothing has been eaten. Shia jurists have their own rulings too. Each school has its reasons, and Muslims follow their own. Fourth, where intention lives. The jurists place it in the heart, not on the tongue; some count waking for the pre-dawn meal as a sign of it. Some say a spoken intention helps focus the mind; others think saying it aloud isn't needed. And the lesson travels: the same act can be two different things, depending on what you meant by it.

1106.title: What breaks it
1106.hook: eating, drinking, intimacy from dawn to sunset; forgetting doesn't break it (Bukhari)
1106.howItsDone: Muslims who are fasting abstain from food, drink and marital intimacy from dawn until sunset; someone who eats or drinks by honest mistake carries on fasting, following the report in Sahih al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, niyyah: intend it. The fast starts in the heart, and the same act can be two things depending on what you meant.

A fasting day, the office kitchen, a full glass of water, and a hand already lifting it halfway before the brain catches up. Or worse: a few swallows gone before anyone remembers. Panic. Is the whole day lost? Do you start over tomorrow, or owe something? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was asked about exactly this, and his answer is gentle. But first, the rules it softens. Today, what breaks the fast, and what doesn't.
screen: `THE OFFICE KITCHEN. A GLASS OF WATER.` → `A FEW SWALLOWS, THEN: WAIT.` → `IS THE DAY LOST?`

segments.voice: First, the frame, from surah two. The fasting believer is told, in Pickthall's words, to "eat and drink until the white thread becometh distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall." The same verse permits marital intimacy in the nights of the fast. So the day runs from the first thread of dawn to sunset, and in those hours the fast is broken by eating, drinking and intimacy. The legal books add details, like deliberately vomiting, and the schools discuss newer questions, but those three are the core. Second, the word that matters is deliberately. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said that if someone fasting forgets and eats or drinks, they should complete their fast, because it was Allah who fed them and gave them drink. Not a failure: a meal from Allah. The fast simply continues. Third, what that answer does. The fast is strict about the clock; dawn means dawn. Yet the person who honestly forgot hasn't broken anything, and yesterday's intention holds. The fast asks for a will, not a flawless memory. Fourth, this week in one breath: the eight doors of zakat, khums in Shia law, giving with dignity, zakat and sadaqah, the many hands, then the turn into the fast, an intention in the heart, and today, rules with mercy built in. And it reaches past the fast: a slip is not the same as a choice.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent slip, small and honest: a promise you forgot, a habit you meant to keep, a word out before you thought. Not something you chose; something that got past you. Look at it plainly, then set it down the way the report sets down the forgotten glass of water, and if you pray, hand it to Allah.
What breaks it. Eating, drinking and intimacy, on purpose, between dawn and sunset. Forgetting doesn't: the one who forgot finishes the fast. Today's word.
